back: Each event is a set of named fields (usually one JSON object per line), with a stable message and the variable parts in fields, so it can be queried without regexes.
Shippers treat each line as an event. A stack trace split across ten lines becomes ten unrelated events; put it in one field.
Factor XI: write logs as an unbuffered event stream to stdout and let the environment collect, route and store them.
One wide structured event per request, written at the end, carrying route, status, duration, IDs and key business fields. Popularised by Stripe.
Passwords, tokens, session cookies, full card numbers and raw personal data. Redact in the shared library with an allow-list of fields.
CVE-2021-44228: Log4j 2 lookups ran on logged strings, so attacker input in a log line led to remote code execution. Logged values are untrusted input.

front: A retry failed once, then succeeded. Level?
back: WARN at most. ERROR means the operation failed for a caller; logging handled exceptions as ERROR trains people to ignore ERROR.

front: Should you page on ERROR log lines?
back: No. Count errors as a metric and alert on the rate. Logs arrive late, scale with traffic, and are the evidence you read after the alert.
A unique ID assigned when a request enters the system, propagated to every call, message and job it causes, and written in every log line.

front: Where does the request ID live inside a service?
back: In request-scoped context: MDC or thread-local in Java, contextvars in Python, context.Context in Go, AsyncLocalStorage in Node.js.

front: Where does correlation-ID propagation usually break?
back: Async hops: queues, thread pools that lose thread-local context, scheduled jobs, and third parties that drop unknown headers.
Elasticsearch/OpenSearch index full text: fast arbitrary search, expensive. Loki indexes only labels and scans compressed chunks: cheap, slower for wide searches.

front: Why must the logging pipeline never block the app?
back: A synchronous network appender turns a slow log store into slow requests. Write async or to a local buffer and drop or spill to disk under pressure.
QPS × lines per request × bytes per line × 86,400. 20,000 × 5 × 500 B × 86,400 = 4.32 TB/day.

front: Why sample logs by request ID, not by line?
back: Line sampling keeps fragments of many requests and the whole story of none. Hashing the request ID keeps every line of the kept requests.

front: When should a log line become a metric?
back: When you only ever count it. A counter costs a few bytes per scrape regardless of traffic; a log line costs its full size every time.
